ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Tampere Region.
Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli.
Participants completed two tasks measuring affective empathy during an EMG recording.
Expecting participants were primarily recruited through the maternity clinics of the City of Tampere.
Fathers of young infants were recruited using contact information of parents of infants born in Tampere and surrounding areas obtained from the Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency.
We presented the tasks to the participants using E-Prime 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA) and participants completed all tasks on a computer in a laboratory setting.
Participants gave their answers on a continuous numerical scale (range 1-9) by clicking a number on the screen after each picture.
The participants gave a saliva sample after receiving information about the study and signing a consent form, before any other measurements.

To control for unwanted variation in testosterone levels, the participants were instructed to refrain from heavy exercise and drinking alcohol for 24 hours, eating or drinking for one hour, and smoking for two hours prior to the study visit.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The current study was part of the TransParent project investigating responses to children's emotion cues during the transition to parenthood (Sinisalo et al., 2022 (Sinisalo et al.,, 2025 (Sinisalo et al.,, 2026;; Veistola et al., 2025; Vuoriainen et al., 2022 Vuoriainen et al.,, 2026)). We ran a cross-sectional laboratory study (N = 118) with three independent groups: expecting men (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and experienced fathers (N = 39). Descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1. We determined the total sample size with a power analysis ('pwr' package; Champely, 2020) to be 100 to reliably detect a small to medium effect size in a general linear model at alpha level 0.05 with statistical power of .80. We collected the data between June 2022 and April 2023. The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Tampere Region.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Pre-registration of Facial Muscle Responses Toward Child-related Emotional Stimuli in Expecting, First-time, and Experienced Fathers
table.research_questions:
a.	Questions:
i.	Do expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers differ in facial muscle responses towards children’s emotional signals?

b.	Hypotheses: 
i.	H1a: Expecting and first-time fathers show greater zygomaticus muscle activation than experienced fathers in response to pictures of children that depict them in positive situations (one-sided).
ii.	H1b: Expecting and first-time fathers differ from each other in zygomaticus muscle activation in response to pictures of children that depict them in positive situations (two-sided).
iii.	H0: Expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers do not differ from each other in zygomaticus muscle activation in response to pictures of children that depict them in positive situations.

iv.	H2a: Expecting and first-time fathers show greater corrugator muscle activation than experienced fathers in response to pictures of children that depict them in negative situations (one-sided).
v.	H2b: Expecting and first-time fathers differ in corrugator muscle activation in response to pictures of children that depict them in negative situations (two-sided).
vi.	H0: Expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers do not differ in corrugator muscle activation in response to pictures of children that depict them in negative situations.

vii.	H3a: Expecting and first-time fathers show greater corrugator muscle activation compared to experienced fathers in response to seeing a video of an infant in danger (one-sided).
viii.	H3b: Expecting and first-time fathers differ in corrugator muscle activation in response to seeing a video of an infant in danger (two-sided).
ix.	H0: Expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers do not differ in corrugator muscle activation in response to seeing a video of an infant in danger.
table.design_dependent_variables:
a.	Task 1 (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022)
i.	Participants viewed 30 images that depict children in naturalistic settings and that vary in emotional valence (negative, neutral, or positive). There were ten images per valence. During viewing these images, participants’ activation of the zygomaticus and corrugator muscles was recorded with electromyography (EMG). 
ii.	Main outcomes:
1.	Zygomaticus activation during viewing positive images.
2.	Corrugator activation when viewing negative images.
iii.	Secondary outcomes:
1.	Self-report of how much compassion and positive affect participants felt when viewing negative and positive images, respectively.
2.	Reduction in zygomaticus activation during viewing negative images.
3.	Reduction in corrugator activation when viewing positive images.
iv.	References
1.	Spencer, H., Lesemann, F., Kraaijenvanger, E., Overbeek, G., Montoya, E., Branje, S., ... & Bos, P. (2022). Oxytocin system gene methylation is associated with empathic responses towards children. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 137, 105629.
2.	Bos, P., Lesemann, F., Spencer, H., Stein, D., van Honk, J., & Montoya, E. (2021). Preliminary data on increased reactivity towards children in distress after testosterone administration in women: A matter of protection?. Biological Psychology, 165, 108176.

b.	Task 2 (Lotz et al., 2021; van ‘t Veer et al., 2019)
i.	Participants watched videos of scenarios in which an infant doll was in a dangerous situation and matched neutral videos without danger to the infant doll. Participants watched 12 different video pairs. Each video was repeated twice resulting in 24 threat and 24 control trials. During viewing these videos, participants’ facial muscle activation was recorded with electromyography (EMG).
ii.	Main outcomes:
1.	Corrugator activation during viewing threat videos.
iii.	Secondary outcome
1.	Reduction in zygomaticus activation during viewing threat videos.
iv.	References
1.	Lotz, A., Verhees, M., Horstman, L., Riem, M., van IJzendoorn, M., Bakermans-Kranenburg, M., & Buisman, R. (2021). Exploring the hormonal and neural correlates of paternal protective behavior to their infants. Developmental Psychobiology, 63, 1358-1369.
2.	van ‘t Veer, A., Thijssen, S., Witteman, J., van IJzendoorn, M., & Bakermans-Kranenburg, M. (2019). Exploring the neural basis for paternal protection: an investigation of the neural response to infants in danger. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 14(4), 447-457.
table.study_design_overview:
i.	There is one within-subject condition with three levels (positive, neutral, and negative) in Task 1.
ii.	There is one within-subject condition with two levels (threat and control) in Task 2.
iii.	Participants belong to one of three independent natural groups: expecting men, first-time fathers, or experienced fathers.
table.statistical_tests:
a.	We will use mixed models with the lme4 and lmer packages in R
b.	Zygomaticus and corrugator activity are the main outcomes
i.	Self-reported ratings of empathy are included in separate, secondary models.
c.	Main predictors (fixed effects) are: Condition, Group, and Time.
d.	For each model, we will use the maximal random effects structure justified by our design and supported by the data, including random slopes for main fixed effects to control for Type 1 errors.
e.	To assess significance, we will use parametric bootstrapping to obtain confidence intervals and Satterthwaite approximation of degrees of freedom to obtain t-tests.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
a.	EMG-data: Trials are rejected as artifacts if the average post-stimulus onset EMG activity is ± 3 SD from the mean activity within subjects.
b.	Across all data: Potential extreme values will be winsorized to 95% confidence intervals with preserved ranking of datapoints to improve the normality of residual distributions. Extreme values are defined as datapoints + or - 3.29 SD from the mean.
table.sample_size:
a.	We determined the original sample size to be 100 to reliably detect a medium effect size. We intended to collect a sample with 50% expecting and 50% fathers. However, due to resource constraints we could not reach our desired sample of expecting men.
b.	The achieved sample sizes:
•	Expecting men N = 35
•	First-time fathers N = 44
•	Experienced fathers N = 39
table.additional_comments:
5.	Secondary questions and analyses
a.	Following questionnaires’ correlations with main outcomes:
i.	Interpersonal Reactivity Index. (IRI; Davis, 1983). 
ii.	Parental Care and Tenderness questionnaire (PCAT; Hofer et al., 2018).
iii.	Paternal Involvement with Infants Scale (PIWIS; Singley et al., 2018).
1.	References:
a.	Davis (1983). Measuring individual differences in empathy: Evidence for a multidimensional approach. Journal of personality and social psychology, 44(1), 113.
b.	Hofer, M., Buckels, E., White, C., Beall, A., & Schaller, M. (2018). Individual differences in activation of the parental care motivational system: An empirical distinction between protection and nurturance. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 9(8), 907 916.
c.	Singley, D. B., Cole, B. P., Hammer, J. H., Molloy, S., Rowell, A., & Isacco, A. (2018). Development and psychometric evaluation of the Paternal Involvement With Infants Scale. Psychology of Men & Masculinity, 19(2), 167.
b.	Testosterone
i.	Our secondary question is whether testosterone (measured with a saliva sample during participants’ laboratory visit) level has an effect on facial muscle responses towards children’s emotional signals.
ii.	We will run a secondary model with testosterone level added and inspect both its main effect and interaction with Group.


A student has pre-processed and run a preliminary analysis of EMG data from Task 1 for their master thesis. The student’s hypothesis and analysis were non-overlapping with this study.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 667 columns across 26 data files.
#### Issues Identified

13 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

438 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **300 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 7 of 26 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  0 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  14 installable dependencies detected.
- 437 statistics stored from the extracted output; 1 of 68 reported tests matched (1.5%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Tampere Region.
live_data_statements: Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli.
Participants completed two tasks measuring affective empathy during an EMG recording.
Expecting participants were primarily recruited through the maternity clinics of the City of Tampere.
Fathers of young infants were recruited using contact information of parents of infants born in Tampere and surrounding areas obtained from the Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency.
We presented the tasks to the participants using E-Prime 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA) and participants completed all tasks on a computer in a laboratory setting.
Participants gave their answers on a continuous numerical scale (range 1-9) by clicking a number on the screen after each picture.
The participants gave a saliva sample after receiving information about the study and signing a consent form, before any other measurements.

To control for unwanted variation in testosterone levels, the participants were instructed to refrain from heavy exercise and drinking alcohol for 24 hours, eating or drinking for one hour, and smoking for two hours prior to the study visit.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("Data_analysis_Study_1.R", 
"Data_analysis_Study_2.r"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**22 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `./demographics.csv` to `Data Study 1/demographics.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./AffEm.csv` to `Data Study 1/AffEm.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./RMET.csv` to `Data Study 1/RMET.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./valence_data.csv` to `Data Study 1/valence_data.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./IRI.csv` to `Data Study 1/IRI.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./PCAT.csv` to `Data Study 1/PCAT.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./TAS.csv` to `Data Study 1/TAS.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./BSI.csv` to `Data Study 1/BSI.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./ABS.csv` to `Data Study 1/ABS.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R); `./PAAS.csv` to `Data Study 1/PAAS.csv` (in Data_analysis_Study_1.R), and 12 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

text.text: Empathy supports effective caregiving, as parents rely on infants' non-verbal signals to guide their responses.
Emerging evidence suggests that men undergo hormonal and neural changes related to empathy during the transition to parenthood.

This study investigated men's empathic reactions towards children by comparing groups at different stages of fatherhood to test a proposal that expecting and first-time fathers show heightened empathic reactivity to children's distress.
With pre-registered analyses, we compared three groups: expecting fathers (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and fathers of more than one child (N = 39).
Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli.
Their facial muscle responses were measured using facial electromyography (zygomaticus and corrugator muscles).
Participants also reported their subjective emotional reactions and provided saliva samples for testosterone assessment.

Only in the Picture task first-time fathers showed stronger corrugator activity to negative child stimuli when compared with expecting fathers, while self-reported empathy did not differentiate the groups.
Testosterone was negatively associated with corrugator responses toward negative pictures of children, but only among expecting fathers.

Although group differences were modest, these findings point to subtle shifts in fathers' responsiveness during the transition to parenthood and indicate that early fatherhood may represent a period of heightened responsiveness to child distress.

Affective empathy, the automatic emotional resonance with another's emotional state (De Waal & Preston, 2017; Singer, & Lamm, 2009), is a crucial element of parenting as it allows parents to simulate their child's emotional experience.
text.formatted: Affective empathy, the automatic emotional resonance with another's emotional state <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Waal & Preston, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Singer, & Lamm, 2009)</ref>, is a crucial element of parenting as it allows parents to simulate their child's emotional experience.

text.text: Children's emotional signals shape parent-child interaction and proximity by motivating empathic reactions to the child's cues (Bell & Ainsworth, 1972; George & Solomon, 2008).
text.formatted: Children's emotional signals shape parent-child interaction and proximity by motivating empathic reactions to the child's cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bell & Ainsworth, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">George & Solomon, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, affective empathy supports parents in recognizing and addressing their preverbal infant's needs, mobilizing protective action in times of threat, and fostering the appropriate, contingent responsiveness that underlies sensitive caregiving (Ainsworth et al., 1978; Bos, Spencer, & Buisman, 2026).
text.formatted: Consequently, affective empathy supports parents in recognizing and addressing their preverbal infant's needs, mobilizing protective action in times of threat, and fostering the appropriate, contingent responsiveness that underlies sensitive caregiving <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ainsworth et al., 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bos, Spencer, & Buisman, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Given that affective empathy operates through rapid, automatic emotional resonance, it is reflected in measurable physiological responses to children's affective signals.

Affective stimuli such as facial expressions or scenes depicting emotionally positive or negative situations elicit rapid, automatic changes in facial muscle activity that are associated with changes in affective states (Kraaijenvanger et al., 2017) and empathic reactions (Braadbaart et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Affective stimuli such as facial expressions or scenes depicting emotionally positive or negative situations elicit rapid, automatic changes in facial muscle activity that are associated with changes in affective states <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kraaijenvanger et al., 2017)</ref> and empathic reactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braadbaart et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Such facial responses to affective stimuli can be measured with facial electromyography (EMG; Cacioppo et al., 1986; Dimberg et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Such facial responses to affective stimuli can be measured with facial electromyography (EMG; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cacioppo et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Dimberg et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Negative affective stimuli typically produce corrugator supercilii (COR) activity in the brow region, associated with frowning and negative affect, while positive affective stimuli elicit zygomaticus major (ZYG) activity in the cheek muscle region, related to smiling and positive affect (Larsen, Norris, & Cacioppo, 2003; Tan et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Negative affective stimuli typically produce corrugator supercilii (COR) activity in the brow region, associated with frowning and negative affect, while positive affective stimuli elicit zygomaticus major (ZYG) activity in the cheek muscle region, related to smiling and positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Larsen, Norris, & Cacioppo, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Tan et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Because these facial muscle responses can reflect rapid, automatic affective reactions to others' emotional expressions, facial EMG has been used as an index of affective responding in research on empathy.

Muscle reactions are fast and automatic: they occur as a response to emotional stimuli even when they are subconscious (Dimberg, Thunberg, & Elmehed, 2000) and when there is attempt to inhibit facial muscle activation (Korb, Grandjean, & Scherer, 2010).
text.formatted: Muscle reactions are fast and automatic: they occur as a response to emotional stimuli even when they are subconscious <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dimberg, Thunberg, & Elmehed, 2000)</ref> and when there is attempt to inhibit facial muscle activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Korb, Grandjean, & Scherer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, research has indicated that individuals with higher levels of self-reported empathy exhibit greater facial muscle activity when observing others' emotions (Dimberg et al., 2011; Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012; Van der Graaff et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Importantly, research has indicated that individuals with higher levels of self-reported empathy exhibit greater facial muscle activity when observing others' emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Dimberg et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Van der Graaff et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These studies assessed empathy using self-report measures, although the specific measures and dimensions of empathy differed across studies.

Moreover, the studies examined responses to both positive and negative emotional stimuli, including happy and angry facial expressions (Dimberg et al., 2011; Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012) and happy and sad emotional stimuli (Van der Graaff et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Moreover, the studies examined responses to both positive and negative emotional stimuli, including happy and angry facial expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Dimberg et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012)</ref> and happy and sad emotional stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Van der Graaff et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study we investigated men's facial muscle activation as a marker of affective empathy and emotional reactivity towards children.
We investigated whether men's facial muscle responses to images of children's emotional signals and situations indicating danger to the child are modulated by men's parental status.

In a cross-sectional design we compared fathers at different points of transition to fatherhood: expecting men (expecting first child), first-time fathers (fathers who had one infant), and experienced fathers (fathers with two or more children).

Becoming a father for the first time is a period marked by significant neural and hormonal changes that are associated with responsiveness to child signals in new fathers (Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019; Kuo et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Becoming a father for the first time is a period marked by significant neural and hormonal changes that are associated with responsiveness to child signals in new fathers <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kuo et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Fathers' physiological changes can begin already during their partner's pregnancy (Diaz-Rojas et al., 2021) and become more pronounced after the child is born (Diaz-Rojas et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Fathers' physiological changes can begin already during their partner's pregnancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Diaz-Rojas et al., 2021)</ref> and become more pronounced after the child is born <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Diaz-Rojas et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kim et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a number of studies have found that men's testosterone declines as they become a father (Gettler, McDade, Feranil, and Kuzawa, 2011; Gray et al., 2002; Meijer et al., 2019; Saxbe et al., 2017), a change that is hypothesized to help the new father to increase their focus on their family and childcare, instead of competition and mating (Archer, 2006; Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2022; Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011 ). Fleming et al. (2002) proposed that, besides shifting men's focus towards parenting, the drop in testosterone during the transition to fatherhood may be associated with changes in responses to infant distress.
text.formatted: For example, a number of studies have found that men's testosterone declines as they become a father <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gettler, McDade, Feranil, and Kuzawa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gray et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Meijer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Saxbe et al., 2017)</ref>, a change that is hypothesized to help the new father to increase their focus on their family and childcare, instead of competition and mating <ref type="bibr">(Archer, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr">). Fleming et al. (2002)</ref> proposed that, besides shifting men's focus towards parenting, the drop in testosterone during the transition to fatherhood may be associated with changes in responses to infant distress.

text.text: They found that, compared with childless men, fathers responded to infant distress with greater self-reported sympathy and urge to help the infant, and that these responses were stronger among fathers with lower testosterone levels (Fleming et al., 2002).
text.formatted: They found that, compared with childless men, fathers responded to infant distress with greater self-reported sympathy and urge to help the infant, and that these responses were stronger among fathers with lower testosterone levels <ref type="bibr">(Fleming et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, testosterone may be involved in motivational processes relevant to parental protection.

Recent theoretical work proposes that caregiving encompasses both nurturant and protective responses, with empathic processes potentially contributing to the motivation to engage in both forms of caregiving (Bos et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent theoretical work proposes that caregiving encompasses both nurturant and protective responses, with empathic processes potentially contributing to the motivation to engage in both forms of caregiving <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bos et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this framework, preliminary results showed that, in women, testosterone administration increased facial EMG reactivity to images of children designed to elicit empathic responses, with the increase appearing strongest in women with higher self-reported protective care motivation (Bos et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Consistent with this framework, preliminary results showed that, in women, testosterone administration increased facial EMG reactivity to images of children designed to elicit empathic responses, with the increase appearing strongest in women with higher self-reported protective care motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that testosterone-related changes may influence both sensitivity to others' emotional states and the mobilization of protective action, processes that are central to parental responses to infant threat ( Van 't Veer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Together, these findings suggest that testosterone-related changes may influence both sensitivity to others' emotional states and the mobilization of protective action, processes that are central to parental responses to infant threat ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Van 't Veer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, the specific effects of testosterone on fathers' empathic responses to children have yet to be studied comprehensively.

The period of expecting and caring for a pre-verbal infant for the first time might represent a phase during which a parent's responsiveness to child signals is particularly heightened (Gettler et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018; Storey et al., 2000).
text.formatted: The period of expecting and caring for a pre-verbal infant for the first time might represent a phase during which a parent's responsiveness to child signals is particularly heightened <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gettler et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Storey et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from mothers suggests that neural responses to infant affective cues are modulated by parity (Maupin et al., 2019; Vuoriainen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Evidence from mothers suggests that neural responses to infant affective cues are modulated by parity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Maupin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Vuoriainen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Compared to multiparous mothers, primiparous mothers showed heightened attention-related neural responses towards infant cues (Bunderson et al., 2020; Maupin et al., 2016) and rated them as higher in subjective emotional arousal (Parsons et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Compared to multiparous mothers, primiparous mothers showed heightened attention-related neural responses towards infant cues <ref type="bibr">(Bunderson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Maupin et al., 2016)</ref> and rated them as higher in subjective emotional arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Parsons et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal evidence further indicates that mothers' early attentional bias toward infant distress diminishes across their child's first year (Hiraoka et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Longitudinal evidence further indicates that mothers' early attentional bias toward infant distress diminishes across their child's first year <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hiraoka et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Enhanced reactivity in first-time parents may serve an adaptive function, focusing attention on infant cues and facilitating the acquisition of parenting skills.
Moreover, biological changes associated with the transition to parenthood may be more pronounced with the first child, potentially resulting in reduced reactivity when caring for subsequent children.
However, it remains unknown whether these hypothesized parity effects characterize fathers as findings from mothers cannot be assumed to directly generalize to fathers.

Although it has now been documented that men undergo physiological changes during transition to parenthood, studies on how fathers' experience as a parent (operationalized as the child's age or the number of children) might modulate their responses to infant emotional cues are currently lacking.
Our previous study (Veistola et al., 2025) addressed this question by comparing childless men, expecting men, and fathers on affective empathy.
text.formatted: Our previous study <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Veistola et al., 2025)</ref> addressed this question by comparing childless men, expecting men, and fathers on affective empathy.

text.text: In a large online sample, we showed the participants images of children in naturalistic, emotional contexts (Spencer et al., 2022) and they self-reported their affective empathy towards the child.

text.text: An unexpected exploratory finding that fathers with multiple children reported lower empathy compared to expecting and first-time fathers prompted us to examine fathers with different amounts of childcare experience more closely in a separate sample.

Overall, in our two samples, we found that fathers expecting a child or living with a young infant showed heightened self-reported affective empathy towards children's emotional cues, as compared to childless men and fathers with older children irrespective of parity (Veistola et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Overall, in our two samples, we found that fathers expecting a child or living with a young infant showed heightened self-reported affective empathy towards children's emotional cues, as compared to childless men and fathers with older children irrespective of parity <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Veistola et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The previous study provided us with initial evidence that the amount of childcare experience a man has might also affect their empathic responses to child cues.
Some evidence suggests that fathers' physiology may differ between first-time and more experienced fathers.
After an initial postnatal decline in testosterone, fathers may show a testosterone rebound as their child grows (Corpuz et al., 2021; Rosenbaum et al., 2018).
text.formatted: After an initial postnatal decline in testosterone, fathers may show a testosterone rebound as their child grows <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Corpuz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rosenbaum et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Testosterone decline may be prolonged in fathers who cohabit with their children (Mascaro et al., 2014), although it remains unclear whether cohabitation itself suppresses the rebound (Gettler et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Testosterone decline may be prolonged in fathers who cohabit with their children <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mascaro et al., 2014)</ref>, although it remains unclear whether cohabitation itself suppresses the rebound <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gettler et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting experience can also influence fathers' immediate physiological reactions to child signals (Fleming et al., 2002; Gettler et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Parenting experience can also influence fathers' immediate physiological reactions to child signals <ref type="bibr">(Fleming et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Gettler et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, first-time fathers were found to show an increase in oxytocin when holding their first-born, while fathers with multiple children showed no change in oxytocin levels between pre-and post-holding (Gettler et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For instance, first-time fathers were found to show an increase in oxytocin when holding their first-born, while fathers with multiple children showed no change in oxytocin levels between pre-and post-holding <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gettler et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, such physiological responses are likely shaped not only by parity but also by the level of involvement and the type of caregiving behavior fathers provide.
Yet, despite initial insights into fathers' physiological changes, direct evidence connecting fathers' childcare experience to empathy-related physiological responses toward children remains scarce.

Investigating how parenting experience shapes fathers' physiological responses is essential for advancing a balanced understanding of human caregiving, especially as fathers' involvement and their influence on child development become increasingly recognized (Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Investigating how parenting experience shapes fathers' physiological responses is essential for advancing a balanced understanding of human caregiving, especially as fathers' involvement and their influence on child development become increasingly recognized <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Building on prior findings that fathers' empathic and physiological responses to child signals may vary with parenting experience, the present study directly examines fathers' physiological reactions to children's emotional cues and threat-related situations.
Specifically, we assessed fathers' empathic responding by measuring facial muscle activation as they viewed children's emotional expressions and scenarios involving potential danger.
Participants completed two tasks measuring affective empathy during an EMG recording.
First, we presented fathers with images of children in naturalistic situations that had either negative, positive, or neutral emotional valence (Picture task; Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, we presented fathers with images of children in naturalistic situations that had either negative, positive, or neutral emotional valence (Picture task; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Spencer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, participants watched videos of lifelike scenarios in which a realistic infant doll was in a threatening or neutral situation (Video task; Lotz et al., 2021; Van 't Veer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Second, participants watched videos of lifelike scenarios in which a realistic infant doll was in a threatening or neutral situation <ref type="bibr">(Video task;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lotz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Van 't Veer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We compared three distinct father groups: expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers.

Expecting fathers were fathers whose partner was expecting their first child, first-time fathers had their first infant and no older children, and experienced fathers were fathers of an infant and one or more older children.

Our main pre-registered research question examined whether expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers differ in their rapid facial muscle responses to children's emotional signals (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2W3SE).
text.formatted: Our main pre-registered research question examined whether expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers differ in their rapid facial muscle responses to children's emotional signals (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2W3SE">https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2W3SE</ref>).

text.text: Zygomaticus responses to positive pictures.

We hypothesized, based on our previous findings (Veistola et al., 2025), that in the Picture task, responding to pictures of children in positive situations, expecting and first-time fathers would exhibit greater activation of the zygomaticus muscle compared to experienced fathers (H1a, one-sided).
text.formatted: We hypothesized, based on our previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Veistola et al., 2025)</ref>, that in the Picture task, responding to pictures of children in positive situations, expecting and first-time fathers would exhibit greater activation of the zygomaticus muscle compared to experienced fathers (H1a, one-sided).

text.text: Additionally, we investigated whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in zygomaticus muscle activation in response to these positive images (H1b, two-sided).
Corrugator responses to negative pictures.

We hypothesized that expecting and first-time fathers would show greater activation of the corrugator muscle than experienced fathers when viewing pictures of children in negative situations (H2a, one-sided).
Again, we also investigated whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in corrugator muscle activation in these negative situations (H2b, two-sided).
text.formatted: Again, we also investigated whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in corrugator muscle activation in these negative situations <ref type="bibr">(H2b, two-sided)</ref>.

text.text: Corrugator responses to infant-danger videos.

Regarding the Video task, we hypothesized that expecting and first-time fathers would demonstrate greater corrugator muscle activation compared to experienced fathers when watching a video of an infant in danger (H3a, one-sided).
We also assessed whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in their corrugator muscle activation in response to the videos depicting danger to the infant (H3b, twosided).
In addition to the pre-registered hypotheses, we conducted several secondary and exploratory analyses.
First, we examined whether salivary testosterone levels were associated with facial EMG responses to emotional child stimuli.

Specifically, we assessed Spearman's rank-order correlations between testosterone levels and corrugator activity in response to negative pictures and zygomaticus activity in response to positive pictures, both across the full sample and within each participant group.
This analysis was preregistered as a secondary analysis.

We also examined associations between facial EMG responses and individual differences in trait empathy (Interpersonal Reactivity Index; IRI), parental care and tenderness (PCAT), and paternal involvement with infants (PIWIS).
These questionnaire-EMG correlations were pre-registered as secondary analyses.
In addition, in exploratory analyses that were not pre-registered, we examined associations with depressive symptoms assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS).

Finally, because the pre-registered analyses of the Video task did not reveal the expected effects of condition, we conducted additional post hoc analyses to examine whether responses might have been temporally localized within specific periods of the videos.
These analyses were not pre-registered and were conducted for descriptive and hypothesis-generating purposes.

The current study was part of the TransParent project investigating responses to children's emotion cues during the transition to parenthood (Sinisalo et al., 2022 (Sinisalo et al., , 2025 (Sinisalo et al., , 2026;; Veistola et al., 2025; Vuoriainen et al., 2022 Vuoriainen et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: The current study was part of the TransParent project investigating responses to children's emotion cues during the transition to parenthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Sinisalo et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Sinisalo et al., , 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Sinisalo et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Veistola et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Vuoriainen et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Vuoriainen et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: We ran a cross-sectional laboratory study (N = 118) with three independent groups: expecting men (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and experienced fathers (N = 39).
Descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: We determined the total sample size with a power analysis ('pwr' package; Champely, 2020) to be 100 to reliably detect a small to medium effect size in a general linear model at alpha level 0.05 with statistical power of .80.
We collected the data between June 2022 and April 2023.
The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Tampere Region.
Expecting participants were primarily recruited through the maternity clinics of the City of Tampere.
Nurses informed fathers about the study during prenatal visits either directly or their pregnant partners were asked to relay the information to the child's father.
The parent received a brief study brochure from the nurse.
Additionally, we distributed study advertisements to the maternity clinics, and the study was advertised through social media.
Fathers of young infants were recruited using contact information of parents of infants born in Tampere and surrounding areas obtained from the Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency.
We sent parents a research brochure by mail or email.

In the research brochure, we requested men interested in study participation to provide their contact information (name, email, and phone number) either directly to the researchers or through a registration form on the project's website.

Upon receiving the contact information, we contacted potential participants by phone to provide further information about the study, ensured that inclusion criteria were met, and arranged the timing of the first research visit.
We included participants who were at least 18 years old, fluent in Finnish, and cohabiting with their child's mother.
Expecting men's pregnant partner was expecting their first child in their third trimester.
Fathers were required to have an approximately 4-month-old infant.
The fathers were further divided into two groups: those with no older children (firsttime fathers) and those with older children (experienced fathers) in addition to the infant.

We excluded participants if they had a diagnosis for a psychiatric or neurological condition, if their infant was born premature or had a congenital disease, or if the participant was using anabolic steroids, given their impact on testosterone levels.
We presented the tasks to the participants using E-Prime 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA) and participants completed all tasks on a computer in a laboratory setting.
Self-report measures were sent to the participant after the visit, and they completed them online on their own time.

To assess participants' facial and self-reported emotional responses to children's positive and negative emotions, we used a task previously developed and employed by Bos and colleagues (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: To assess participants' facial and self-reported emotional responses to children's positive and negative emotions, we used a task previously developed and employed by Bos and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Spencer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The task uses grayscale images of children in naturalistic situations and has previously been used to investigate empathic responses towards children, combining facial electromyographic responses with self-reported ratings of compassion and positive affect (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022; Veistola et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The task uses grayscale images of children in naturalistic situations and has previously been used to investigate empathic responses towards children, combining facial electromyographic responses with self-reported ratings of compassion and positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Spencer et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Veistola et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The images depicted children in negative (e.g., a child crying alone on the street), positive (e.g., a child playing with a parent), or neutral (e.g., a child sitting at a dining table) situations.
There were 10 images of each valence, that were presented for two seconds in a random order.
Each image was preceded by a fixation cross (1 s).
In total, the participants viewed 30 images.
The images were each followed by two questions (self-paced), resulting in 60 self-report responses.
Participants gave their answers on a continuous numerical scale (range 1-9) by clicking a number on the screen after each picture.
The first question measured positive affect: "How positive do you feel about the picture?"
(1 = not at all positive,9 = very positive).
The second question measured compassion: "How much compassion do you feel for the child?"
(1 = not at all,9 = very much).
There was no time limit for the response, and response latency was recorded but not included as a covariate because the self-report responses occurred after the predefined EMG measurement windows.
We did not form hypotheses regarding the response latency.
To assess participants' facial empathic reactions towards threat to an infant, in the second task participants viewed threatening and neutral videos.

We used a video task that has previously been used to investigate responses to infants in threatening versus neutral situations in the context of paternal protection, including with neuroimaging and hormonal measures (Lotz et al., 2021; van 't Veer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We used a video task that has previously been used to investigate responses to infants in threatening versus neutral situations in the context of paternal protection, including with neuroimaging and hormonal measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lotz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">van 't Veer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, it has not previously been used or validated for assessing facial electromyographic responses.

In the task, participants watched 12 videos of scenarios in which a lifelike infant doll was in a threatening situation (e.g., in a pram that slides into a canal) and 12 matched neutral videos in which the context was identical but there was no threat to the infant doll (e.g., in a pram that is safely parked next to a canal).
Each video lasted 6 seconds and was repeated twice resulting in 24 threat and 24 control trials.
The trials were separated into two blocks containing only threat or control videos.
We used a blocked instead of a randomized presentation because frequency-based EEG and heart rate measures were also collected during the task (not reported here).
Each video was preceded by a fixation cross (1 s).
The blocks were presented in the same order for all participants, with the threat video block presented first, followed by the control video block.
Within the video blocks, the individual videos were presented in random order.
We placed two pairs of Ag/AgCl electrodes on the left side of the participant's face, following established guidelines for facial EMG recording (Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986).
text.formatted: We placed two pairs of Ag/AgCl electrodes on the left side of the participant's face, following established guidelines for facial EMG recording <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: One pair was attached over the corrugator supercilii muscle (COR; next to the eyebrow) and the other pair over the zygomaticus major muscle (ZYG; on the cheek between the ear and corner of the mouth) for muscle activation (EMG) measurement.
Each pair's electrodes were placed 1 cm apart from each other.
A ground electrode was attached on top of the participant's seventh cervical vertebra (C7).
Before attaching the electrodes, the skin was gently rubbed with disinfectant, and the electrodes were filled with conductive electrolyte gel (Signa gel).
EMG signals were sampled at 1000 Hz using an actiCHamp Plus (Brain Products GmbH) amplifier.

Offline, we pre-processed the data with BrainVision Analyzer 2.2. and R Statistical Software (v 4.4.1, R Core Team, 2024), following recommendations for EMG signal acquisition and processing (Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986; Rutkowska et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Offline, we pre-processed the data with BrainVision Analyzer 2.2. and R Statistical Software (v 4.4.1, R Core Team, 2024), following recommendations for EMG signal acquisition and processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Rutkowska et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The raw data were first band-pass filtered at 28-499 Hz with a notch filter of 50 Hz and then rectified.
For the Picture task, we segmented data for each 2 s trial into 250-ms time bins time-locked to stimulus onset, resulting in 8 time bins.
For the Video task, we segmented the data for each 6 s trial into 500-ms time bins time-locked to stimulus onset, resulting in 12 time bins.
For both tasks, we used a 1 s baseline preceding each stimulus.
One participant from the expectant fathers' group was removed due to missing data resulting from a technical error during the EMG data recording during the Video task.
Thus, the Video task analyses were done with 117 participants.
For every participant, muscle, and time bin, we calculated that participant's average EMG activation and its standard deviation across all conditions.
Each EMG value was then compared to the mean from its own participant-muscle-time-bin combination, and values more than three standard deviations above this reference were marked as artifacts.
There is no single established criterion for artifact rejection in facial EMG, and different thresholds and procedures have been used in previous studies (Rutkowska et al., 2024).
text.formatted: There is no single established criterion for artifact rejection in facial EMG, and different thresholds and procedures have been used in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Rutkowska et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Visual inspection indicated that the data were relatively clean, and we therefore selected a threshold intended to limit the removal of plausible facial muscle activity while identifying prominent artifacts, such as eye blinks.
With the aforementioned criterion, 1.38% of the data from the Picture task was detected as artifacts.
The number of artifacts did not differ between the time bins, F(8) = 0.32, p = .959, nor between groups, F(2) = .51, p = .599.
From the Video task, 1.37% of the data was detected as artifacts.
The number of artifacts did not differ between the time bins, F(12) = 0.60, p = .846.
The artifacts differed between groups, F(2) = 6.10, p = .002, however, the differences were very small in practice.
Closer inspection showed that the experienced fathers' group had 0.17% more artifacts compared to first-time fathers, and 0.26% more artifacts compared to expecting fathers.
We removed only the individual time bins flagged as artifacts, while retaining all other time bins within the same trial.
After removing time bins with artifacts, we standardized EMG activity for each participant, muscle, and time bin.
We calculated a participant's mean and standard deviation of EMG activity across all conditions.
We then converted each EMG value into a z-score using the mean and standard deviation from its own participant-muscle-time-bin combination.
We performed baseline correction on these z-scored values by subtracting the z-scored activity in the 1000 ms pre-stimulus baseline window from the post-stimulus time bins.
We used these standardized, baseline-corrected values as outcomes in the linear mixed-effects models.
Participants' baseline testosterone was measured from saliva samples.
The participants gave a saliva sample after receiving information about the study and signing a consent form, before any other measurements.

To control for unwanted variation in testosterone levels, the participants were instructed to refrain from heavy exercise and drinking alcohol for 24 hours, eating or drinking for one hour, and smoking for two hours prior to the study visit.
The samples were collected with a Salivette® (Sarstedt, Nümbrecht, Germany) polypropylene swab.
Participants chewed the swab for one minute and then inserted the swab into a polyethylene container without touching the swab with their hands or the container with their mouth.
The swab was initially stored at -20 to -30°C before being transported in dry ice to a liquid nitrogen freezer (-80°C).

Salivary testosterone was analyzed with enzyme immunoassay for the quantitative determination of free testosterone in saliva (EIA, IBL International, RE52631) in the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health (Helsinki, Finland).
Assay performance characteristics are reported in the manufacturer's instructions for use (IBL International GmbH, 2025).

text.text: Before hypothesis testing, we examined whether the task worked as intended, i.e., whether the task conditions produced responses in expected direction reflected in facial EMG and evaluative responses.

For the Picture task, we examined the effect of affective condition by including EMG data (COR and ZYG) and ratings (compassion and positive affect) into separate models with affective condition (negative vs. positive vs. neutral) as a fixed effect.
For EMG data analyses, we added time as a fixed factor in interaction with affective condition.
As random effects, we included intercepts for participants, as well as by-participant slopes for condition.
This resulted in the following base model for the Picture task: EMG data / Ratings ~ 1 + Condition * Time + (1 + Condition | Participant).
For the Video task, we examined the effect of the threat video condition by including EMG data (for the COR) into a model with video condition (control vs. threat) as a fixed effect.
Time was added as a fixed factor in interaction with video condition.
As random effects, we included intercepts for participants, as well as by-participant slopes for condition.
This resulted in the following base model: EMG data ~ 1 + Condition * Time + (1 + Condition | Participant).

Across the full sample, in the Picture task, testosterone was not significantly correlated with corrugator responses toward negative images, r s = -0.11, p = .233, nor with zygomatic responses toward positive images, r s = -0.15, p = .100.

Within the expecting fathers' group, testosterone was significantly negatively correlated with corrugator responses toward negative images, r s = -0.50, p = .002, indicating that higher testosterone levels were associated with reduced corrugator responses.
The correlation between testosterone and zygomatic responses in this group was not significant, r s = -0.28, p = .108.
In the first-time father group, we found no significant correlations between testosterone and either corrugator, r s = 0.06, p = .694, or zygomatic responses, r s = 0.05, p = .744.
Similarly, in the experienced group, testosterone was not significantly associated with corrugator, r s = -0.01, p = .957, or zygomaticus responses, r s = -0.23, p = .166.
Empathy plays an important role in caregiving and the moment-to-moment interactions between a caregiver and a non-verbal infant.

The primary aim of this study was to examine whether paternal group membership (expecting, first-time and experienced fathers) is associated with facial EMG responses and self-reported empathy to affective child stimuli.
Overall, the hypothesized group differences were small but partly in line with our hypotheses.
We used a task that has been previously linked to EMG responses with robust condition effects (Spencer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We used a task that has been previously linked to EMG responses with robust condition effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Spencer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As in previous studies, the affective condition produced the expected pattern of facial muscle responses, with positive child emotion displays producing greater zygomaticus responses and negative child emotions producing greater increase in corrugator activity across the three father groups (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As in previous studies, the affective condition produced the expected pattern of facial muscle responses, with positive child emotion displays producing greater zygomaticus responses and negative child emotions producing greater increase in corrugator activity across the three father groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Spencer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The pre-registered planned comparisons showed that first-time fathers exhibited a greater corrugator response toward negative emotions in children than expecting fathers, whereas the difference between experienced and first-time fathers was marginal and did not reach the pre-set significance threshold.
For zygomaticus responses, we could observe a similar pattern, although the grouprelated differences were marginal and did not reach our pre-set significance thresholds.

Selfreported compassion and positive affect varied by affective condition in the expected directions, but did not differ by group, suggesting that paternal status did not influence subjective emotional and empathic experience strongly enough in this study.
Beyond facial EMG and self-reports, hormonal analyses showed that salivary testosterone levels were generally unrelated to facial muscle reactivity in the full sample.
However, within the expecting group, higher testosterone was associated with reduced corrugator responses to negative stimuli.
At present, evidence on how testosterone relates to emotion-related facial muscle responses is limited, and findings from related measures are mixed.

An experimental study in women reported increased affective facial responding following testosterone administration (Bos et al., 2021), whereas other work has linked higher administered or endogenous testosterone levels to lower empathic or affective responses to others' emotions (e.g., Hermans et al., 2006; Procyshyn et al., 2020), often in interaction with other hormones (Zilioli et al., 2015).
text.formatted: An experimental study in women reported increased affective facial responding following testosterone administration <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021)</ref>, whereas other work has linked higher administered or endogenous testosterone levels to lower empathic or affective responses to others' emotions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hermans et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Procyshyn et al., 2020)</ref>, often in interaction with other hormones <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Zilioli et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide evidence for both positive and negative associations between testosterone and emotional responding, making strong directional predictions difficult.
The prior experimental study was conducted in women and not in men transitioning to fatherhood, a period in which the role of testosterone remains debated (Meijer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The prior experimental study was conducted in women and not in men transitioning to fatherhood, a period in which the role of testosterone remains debated <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Meijer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, our findings are not inconsistent with either direction of association reported previously, but they tentatively suggest that testosterone may be particularly relevant for emotional responding in expecting fathers.

Lower testosterone in expecting fathers might be particularly helpful considering evidence that lower prenatal testosterone levels have been associated with greater partner-and child-directed investment in men (Rilling et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Lower testosterone in expecting fathers might be particularly helpful considering evidence that lower prenatal testosterone levels have been associated with greater partner-and child-directed investment in men <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Rilling et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of correlations between testosterone and EMG responses in first-time and experienced fathers might also suggest that testosterone's role in transition to fatherhood may be temporary and subside over time (Corpuz, D'Alessandro, & Collom, 2021).
text.formatted: The absence of correlations between testosterone and EMG responses in first-time and experienced fathers might also suggest that testosterone's role in transition to fatherhood may be temporary and subside over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Corpuz, D'Alessandro, & Collom, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, we did not observe differences in testosterone levels among the three father groups in our sample, even though previous longitudinal studies have documented decreases in testosterone across the transition to fatherhood (Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011).
text.formatted: Notably, we did not observe differences in testosterone levels among the three father groups in our sample, even though previous longitudinal studies have documented decreases in testosterone across the transition to fatherhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation is that our study lacks a comparison group of childless men.
Expectant fathers may have already experienced some reduction in testosterone, making them indistinguishable from the father groups.
In addition, our sample is relatively small and cross-sectional, which limits statistical power compared with longitudinal designs.
Our sample size is particularly relevant for testosterone given that its documented decline tends to be modest in magnitude (Meijer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Our sample size is particularly relevant for testosterone given that its documented decline tends to be modest in magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Meijer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these results suggest that while emotional reactivity to affective stimuli was robust and follows well-established patterns (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022), paternal group differences were subtle and primarily evident in physiological rather than selfreported measures.
text.formatted: Taken together, these results suggest that while emotional reactivity to affective stimuli was robust and follows well-established patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Spencer et al., 2022)</ref>, paternal group differences were subtle and primarily evident in physiological rather than selfreported measures.

text.text: We interpret the greater corrugator responsivity as greater empathic reactivity to children's distress in first-time fathers.

First-time parenthood is a developmental transition during which major changes in social roles and neurobiological functioning take place, supporting adjustment to the parental role (Feldman, 2015; Rilling & Mascaro, 2017; Saxbe et al., 2018).
text.formatted: First-time parenthood is a developmental transition during which major changes in social roles and neurobiological functioning take place, supporting adjustment to the parental role <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feldman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Rilling & Mascaro, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Saxbe et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Our results showed enhanced facial responses specifically to children's negative emotions, which can function as salient signals of distress and need for caregiving.

Consistent with the interpretation of greater empathic reactivity in first-time fathers, a recent study reported greater corrugator responses to distressed faces in first-time mothers than nonmothers (Sinisalo et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Consistent with the interpretation of greater empathic reactivity in first-time fathers, a recent study reported greater corrugator responses to distressed faces in first-time mothers than nonmothers <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Sinisalo et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Enhanced reactivity to negative child signals at the early stages of transitioning to parenthood may therefore reflect increased sensitivity to children's signals that motivate protective or caregiving responses, ensuring that the child's needs are met and the caregiver's resources are allocated to the survival of the infant (Feldman, 2015; Rilling & Mascaro, 2017).
text.formatted: Enhanced reactivity to negative child signals at the early stages of transitioning to parenthood may therefore reflect increased sensitivity to children's signals that motivate protective or caregiving responses, ensuring that the child's needs are met and the caregiver's resources are allocated to the survival of the infant <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feldman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Rilling & Mascaro, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We found greater corrugator responses towards negative emotions specifically in first-time fathers compared to expecting fathers.

We think this difference might emerge since, although expectant men begin to show subtle neurobiological changes during their partner's pregnancy (Diaz-Rojas, 2021), the neurobiological adjustments associated with the transition to parenthood tend to concentrate on the postnatal period for most fathers (Diaz-Rojas, 2023;
Bakermans-Kranenburg, 2019).
Moreover, postnatal neurobiological changes in fathers depend on the amount of time spent on caregiving and the degree of exposure to their infant (Abrahams et al., 2014; Horstman et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, postnatal neurobiological changes in fathers depend on the amount of time spent on caregiving and the degree of exposure to their infant <ref type="bibr">(Abrahams et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Horstman et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the timing of neurobiological changes may help explain why postnatal fathers displayed heightened reactions to child signals compared to antenatal fathers, reflected here in their facial electromyographic responses.
Our results on the self-reported measures contrast those of Veistola et al. (2025) who found significant group differences in self-reported empathy at different stages of fatherhood.
text.formatted: Our results on the self-reported measures contrast those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Veistola et al. (2025)</ref> who found significant group differences in self-reported empathy at different stages of fatherhood.

text.text: Namely, that study found that first-time fathers and expecting fathers reported more empathy (i.e., greater compassion) toward children in distressing situations using the same Picture task.
However, the effect sizes were small, so not replicating these findings in our much smaller sample could be expected.

The marginal and group-specific nature of the effects we found in the current study underscores the complexity of fatherhood-related changes and highlights the need for further research to clarify when and how these differences emerge.
It is not fully clear why the expected condition effects were not observed in the Video task, but several methodological features may have contributed.
First, we presented the emotional and neutral videos in separate blocks with relatively short inter-stimulus intervals.

Although each trial included a 1000-ms pre-stimulus baseline, this interval may not have been sufficient for participants to return to an affectively neutral state after viewing emotionally intense clips, potentially leading to carryover effects.
Second, unlike static images, the threatening content in the videos unfolded over time; in many clips, several seconds elapsed before the threatening event occurred.
Because our EMG analyses were time-locked to video onset rather than to the exact moment when the threat occurred, early neutral segments may have diluted condition differences.
Together, these features may have reduced the sensitivity of the Video task to detect condition-related EMG responses.

A strength of this study is the multi-method approach combining EMG, hormonal measures, and self-reports, as well as precise control over the timing of fathers' participation at different stages of fatherhood.
However, some limitations warrant caution.

Although the Video task has been used previously in research on paternal protection and its neural and hormonal correlates (Lotz et al., 2021; van 't Veer et al., 2019), its ability to elicit facial electromyographic responses has not been established.

text.text: Thus, the null EMG findings should be interpreted considering this limitation.
Further, we did not have a group of childless men which means that we cannot compare the father groups to men who have not undergone the transition to fatherhood.
This limits our ability to detect potential changes that may have already taken place among expecting men.
Our sample was quite homogeneous in terms of socioeconomic background and generalizing these findings should be done with caution.

In the current study, first-time fathers exhibited greater corrugator responses to children's negative emotions compared to expecting fathers, and they also tended to show greater responses than experienced fathers.
To better understand how these differences emerge, future research should consider including a comparison group of childless men in cross-sectional designs.
Such a group would help clarify which changes are specifically linked to the transition into fatherhood.
However, an even more informative next step would be longitudinal research beginning before pregnancy or the intention to become a parent.
Longitudinal designs are essential for identifying within-person changes across the transition to fatherhood and for distinguishing anticipatory processes from experience-driven changes.

In addition, future work should incorporate measures of fathers' day-to-day caregiving involvement to better understand the role of caregiving experience in shaping changes in emotion-related facial muscle activity.
